assessment.security_status_cs: Situace v Rudém moři a oblasti Bab al-Mandab zůstává vysoce napjatá navzdory postupnému návratu části ropných toků a plánům kontejnerových aliancí na návrat k trasám přes Suez. Útoky neznámých projektilů na tankery v Hormuzském průlivu a eskalace pozemních bojů v Jemenu nicméně nadále udržují vysokou prémii za geopolitické riziko v klíčových námořních koridorech.
assessment.security_status_en: The situation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab region remains highly tense despite the gradual return of some oil flows and container alliances planning to resume Suez routes. However, attacks by unknown projectiles on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and escalating ground fighting in Yemen continue to sustain a high geopolitical risk premium in key maritime corridors.

recommendations.reason_cs: Návrat některých dopravců k trase přes Suezský průliv snižuje příjmy z delších plaveb kolem Ohnivého mysu, ale bezpečnostní rizika v regionu stále brání plnému optimismu.
recommendations.reason_en: The return of some carriers to the Suez Canal route reduces revenues from longer Cape of Good Hope voyages, but ongoing security risks in the region prevent full optimism.

recommendations.sector_cs: Obranný průmysl (např. RTX, Lockheed Martin, BAE Systems)
recommendations.sector_en: Defense Industry (e.g. RTX, Lockheed Martin, BAE Systems)
recommendations.reason_cs: Pokračující konflikty na Blízkém východě, útoky na tankery a napětí v Jemenu a na Ukrajině udržují vysokou poptávku po protivzdušné obraně a vojenském vybavení.
recommendations.reason_en: Ongoing Middle East conflicts, attacks on tankers, and tension in Yemen and Ukraine maintain high demand for air defense and military equipment.

recommendations.sector_cs: Ropa a Plyn (např. Shell, BP, Chevron)
recommendations.reason_cs: Ceny ropy klesly v reakci na obnovení exportu z Perského zálivu, avšak přetrvávající hrozby pro námořní dopravu a riziko eskalace brání výraznějšímu poklesu.
recommendations.reason_en: Oil prices have dropped in response to restored Persian Gulf exports, but persistent threats to maritime shipping and escalation risks prevent a steeper decline.

recommendations.sector_cs: Evropský Spotřební sektor & Autoprůmysl (např. Volvo, BMW)
recommendations.reason_cs: Potenciální zkrácení námořních tras může snížit náklady na logistiku, automobilový a spotřební sektor však nadále čelí tlakům vysokých cen energií a slabší poptávce.
recommendations.reason_en: Potential shortening of maritime routes may lower logistics costs, but the automotive and consumer sectors continue to face high energy price pressures and softer demand.

recommendations.sector_cs: Pražská burza: ČEZ, Komerční banka, Erste Group
recommendations.sector_en: Prague Stock Exchange: ČEZ, Komerční banka, Erste Group
recommendations.reason_cs: Domácí tituly jsou pod vlivem globálního výprodeje dluhopisů a makroekonomické nejistoty, fundamenty bank a energetiky však zůstávají stabilní.
recommendations.reason_en: Domestic equities are pressured by the global bond sell-off and macroeconomic uncertainty, though banking and energy fundamentals remain stable.

recommendations.sector_cs: Evropské blue-chips (např. Airbus, TotalEnergies, Allianz, Rheinmetall)
recommendations.sector_en: European blue-chips (e.g. Airbus, TotalEnergies, Allianz, Rheinmetall)
recommendations.reason_cs: Různorodé portfolio evropských gigantů těží z poptávky po obraně a energetice, ale čelí protivětru v podobě globální makroekonomické nestability a růstu výnosů dluhopisů.
recommendations.reason_en: A diverse portfolio of European giants benefits from defense and energy demand, but faces headwinds from global macroeconomic instability and rising bond yields.

assessment.forecast_cs: V nejbližších dnech lze očekávat pokračování potyček v oblasti Rudého moře a Hormuzského průlivu, přičemž trhy budou nadále citlivě reagovat na jakékoliv zprávy o obnovení plného provozu přes Suez.
assessment.forecast_en: Over the coming days, skirmishes in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz are expected to continue, with markets remaining highly sensitive to any news regarding the full resumption of traffic through Suez.
assessment.forecast_review_cs: Předchozí předpověď se potvrdila; intenzivní boje v Jemenu pokračují, tlak na diplomatická řešení roste a ceny ropy nadále vykazují volatilitu kvůli bezpečnostním rizikům v koridorech.
assessment.forecast_review_en: The previous forecast was confirmed; intensive fighting in Yemen continues, pressure for diplomatic solutions is rising, and oil prices continue to exhibit volatility due to security risks in the corridors.

articles.title: South Lebanon: 'It's torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes'
articles.summary:
South Lebanon: 'It's torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes'

Submitted by Laurent Perpigna Iban on Wed, 09/30/2026 - 11:10
Residents of the village of Mansouri are watching helplessly as the Israeli military methodically destroys their town
Standing on a hill in the Hanniyeh village in south Lebanon, people from neighbouring Mansouri watch as Israeli occupation forces raze their village (Laurent Iban Perpigna/MEE)
Off

Day after day, the Israeli-occupied village of Mansouri, perched on a green hill a few kilometres south of the coastal city of Tyre, is slowly disappearing. Already heavily damaged during the war, it is now quite literally being wiped off the map, in a final twist of cynicism, during the ceasefire.

The Israeli army, which has made it one of its main theatres of operations for weeks, is sparing no effort: demolitions with explosives and air strikes have followed one another at a relentless pace in recent days, to the despair of the village’s roughly 5,000 inhabitants.

The village, which the Israeli army presents as an operational stronghold of Hezbollah, was initially located outside the “Yellow Line”, the “security” demarcation imposed by Israel on Lebanese territory shortly after the latest ceasefire came into effect.

Even then, residents Middle East Eye spoke to following the ceasefire feared that the zone would eventually swallow up their village. It now has, although officially only in part: the Yellow Line cuts through Mansouri, dividing it in two.

On paper, that is, as the village is now entirely occupied – this summer, all the residents who had returned to the area had no choice but to flee once again, under fire from the Israeli air force, which continues its operations.

The village mayor has denounced in the local press “attacks against residents using artillery, as well as hand grenades and stun grenades dropped by drones”. He himself miraculously survived after being wounded in an Israeli attack.

My house is the only one still standing

The green road leading to the village of Hanniyeh, still accessible by car to Lebanese civilians, smells of fear.

This tiny village, also perched on a hill outside the Yellow Line, offers an unobstructed view of Mansouri. And, opposite it, of the Israeli troops that have taken up positions on the other side, leaving local residents within firing range.

'This land is everything to us. We will come back and rebuild, God willing'

- Ibtissem, Mansouri resident

And while most of Hanniyeh's residents have chosen to remain displaced further north, dozens of people from Mansouri pass through the village every day, watching in dismay as the Israeli military destroys their hometown.

On the roadside, hidden behind a tree, Ahmad, 47, has set his phone on a tripod. He is livestreaming on Facebook, trying to document the ongoing destruction for a few dozen viewers.

“Look! The yellow house is mine. It’s the only one still standing; all the others around it have been destroyed,” he tells Middle East Eye.

The scene is chilling, dystopian. He admits it himself: watching his village being destroyed every day while waiting for his own house to be next is profoundly disturbing. 

As though the war and Israeli chaos in Lebanon had become a spectacle.

Beside him, Ali, another Mansouri resident whose house was destroyed during the war, says: “Yes, it is humiliating to watch this, but I want to stay here, as close to my village as possible. I don’t want to abandon it.”

He continues: “It’s worse than anything. I no longer have work. I had farmland below the village. Look, smoke is coming from there: they are burning my land.”

Around a hundred metres away, some 30 people, men and women, have set up chairs. Most are neighbours, lifelong friends. Together, they too watch the unspeakable unfold, commenting on the scenes of recent days. 

Now without jobs and unable to access their homes, they kill time according to the rhythm of Israeli operations.

One of them shows a video filmed in recent days: an Israeli drone can be seen very slowly lowering explosives, suspended vertically from a cable, and placing them on a rooftop. The images are striking: a few minutes later, the area explodes.

Suddenly, everyone falls silent. A cloud of dust moves along one of the village streets. Israeli vehicles are coming down the road, kicking up dust as they move.

Looking through binoculars, one of the men says he can see a tractor clearing the rubble of a house, which will soon have been reduced to an empty plot of land.

“We haven’t seen any Merkava tanks today. They must be resting,” jokes a man in his sixties.

Ibtissem, a 38-year-old woman, continues: “Every day something happens. One day they bomb, the next they send bulldozers. Sometimes charges they have planted inside our homes explode. It’s torture, they are razing our lives before our eyes.  

“But this land is everything to us. We will come back and rebuild, God willing,” she says.

Abandoned by everyone

Unsurprisingly, the inaction of the international community, and above all that of the Lebanese government, comes up again and again in every conversation.

Here, the Lebanese army is nowhere to be seen. Worse still, the residents of Mansouri, like those of the 63 villages located in the area occupied by the Israeli army south of the “Yellow Line” – around 460 square kilometres – say they have been completely left to fend for themselves.

This summer, residents organised a peaceful sit-in near the Lebanese army checkpoint in al-Amiriya, under the slogan “Mansouri is not occupied”, calling for an end to the bombardments and for the Lebanese army to return to the village, and saying they were ready to march alongside it as soon as it decided to enter Mansouri.

“Nothing happened. We and our village were abandoned. And since then, nobody has helped us, absolutely nobody, while we remain displaced and no one has work anymore,” sighs one resident.

'It’s worse than anything...Look, smoke is coming from there: they are burning my land'

- Ali, resident of Mansouri

Speaking quietly, almost reluctantly, he admits that even Hezbollah, which for years, war after war, helped affected communities, no longer has the means to do much of anything today.

Today, Mansouri, like Tallouseh and Mais al-Jabal further east, is one of the main theatres of Israeli military operations. Many Lebanese see this as an attempt to “finish the job” – in other words, to destroy any possibility of residents returning to the area in order to consolidate Israel’s presence on the ground for the long term.

This dynamic is continuing despite the 26 June framework agreement, which provided for a different arrangement to be tested in the south.

In Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, three “pilot zones”, the Lebanese army was supposed to gradually regain control on the ground, secure the villages and prevent any unauthorised armed presence there, under the coordination of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon (MCG4L), the US-led mechanism tasked with overseeing the agreement.

The reality, however, is different.

In Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, Israeli soldiers were recently accused of opening fire near Lebanese troops as they deployed. On 18 September, in Deir Mimas, an Israeli force approached a Lebanese army position and threw stun grenades in the vicinity, triggering another face-off, defused in extremis through the intervention of the MCG4L.

“We no longer trust anyone to come and help us,” Abbas, a 26-year-old from Hanniyeh, says with tears in his eyes.

“My dream is to get my land back, my neighbours, to rebuild my house. I don’t have much hope left. To have any, the Lebanese army would need to be capable of holding the ground, and as long as the international community does not put pressure on Israel, we may never see our land again.”

Hanniyeh, Lebanon

articles.title: The West wants Netanyahu gone - so Palestinians can be killed more quietly again
articles.summary:
The West wants Netanyahu gone - so Palestinians can be killed more quietly again

Submitted by Jonathan Cook on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 14:28
Trump, nosediving in the polls and bristling over a disastrous war on Iran, needs a scapegoat – and the Israeli prime minister best fits the bill
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu walks away after addressing the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US on 24 September 2026 (Reuters)
On

Benjamin Netanyahu’s whirlwind visit to the United States last week to address the United Nations General Assembly was further evidence that the Israeli prime minister is now a universal pariah.

He is being abandoned even by his closest allies.

It was perhaps not surprising that 77 nations, including a handful of European states, walked out of the chamber in protest that a wanted war crimes suspect - a fugitive from the International Criminal Court (ICC) - was being given a platform to speak on the world’s largest stage.

Far more notable was what happened - or rather, didn’t - away from the podium. Netanyahu spent just eight hours in the US before heading back to Israel. It is hard to believe that that was his choice. 

He was denied his usual moment in the sun with Donald Trump at the White House, and could not even secure a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

There was no invitation to address the US Congress, and with it familiar scenes of legislators rapturously celebrating his anti-Palestinian incitement. 

Israel's former ambassador to Washington, Michael Oren, told Reuters: "I don't recall a time when the prime minister came to the United States and didn't meet with the president.” 

The shunning of Netanyahu stood in stark contrast to the reception of Xi Jinping. The Chinese leader was personally greeted at the airport by Trump with a red carpet and military flyover.

Warnings ignored

Netanyahu’s UN visit was exploited by both sides - by Israeli officials and western leaders - to advance their separate, and conflicting, agendas.

Netanyahu is a month away from a hotly contested general election in which, for the first time, his failures to prevent Hamas’s attack on 7 October 2023 are under intense scrutiny. 

Britain's settlement trade ban is cosmetic. For it to work, it must sanction Israel
Read More »

According to a growing number of recent reports, he was warned by Egyptian and Gulf leaders of a major event - an “earthquake” - coming from Gaza in the days and weeks preceding Hamas’ breakout, but failed to act.

Netanyahu had scheduled his UN speech for Israeli prime time, to attract the largest domestic audience possible. He took the opportunity to call out other world leaders as “moral cowards” and “hypocrites”. 

As Israeli analyst Jonathan Ofir notes, Netanyahu also used the UN platform to smuggle in a biblical phrase in Hebrew that was designed, for listeners back home, to serve as a dog-whistle: a call for Israel to carry out genocide to the bitter end.

Netanyahu’s goal was to demonstrate to voters that he is still a force to be reckoned with on the international stage, and that he alone can make Israel safe from a world supposedly mired in “antisemitic”, anti-Israel sentiment. 

Western leaders, by contrast, wish to demonstrate the precise opposite, hoping to nudge Netanyahu out of office by suggesting to Israelis that their leader is a spent force, that he has gone too far. 

Time to be rid of him.

This may prove no simple matter. Netanyahu is the great political survivor, serving a record near-two decades as his country’s prime minister - longer even than Israel’s founding father, David Ben Gurion. He has used that time to whip up much of Israeli society into an ever greater, ultra-nationalist, genocidal fervour. 

Political liability

The current antipathy in western capitals to Netanyahu is most certainly not based on any kind of ethical assessment of Israel’s recent actions: a three-year genocidal rampage through Gaza; the violent expansion of Jewish settlements and ethnic cleansing in the Occupied West Bank; the bombing and ethnic cleansing of south Lebanon; and the Israeli leader’s starring role alongside the US in launching a catastrophic war on Iran whose fallout has destabilised the global economy.

Washington - backed by its European client states  - has been an ardent partner to these crimes, supplying the munitions, intelligence and diplomatic leverage to help Israel carry them out. 

The current antipathy in western capitals to Netanyahu is most certainly not based on any kind of ethical assessment of Israel’s recent actions

But Netanyahu now looks to be a political liability, even for Trump.

The US president, nosediving in the polls, needs a scapegoat – and the Israeli prime minister appears the only one suited for the role. 

The antagonism is, in part, personal. 

A number of recent reports indicate that Netanyahu pulled out all the stops to seduce Trump, against the advice of his generals, into launching an unprovoked and illegal war on Iran. 

The promise of a decisive victory persuaded Trump he could secure his place in the history books as the president who “remade the Middle East”. Once Iran was out of the picture, the US would enjoy unchallenged control over the region’s oil. 

And all of this would supposedly take place weeks after Trump had cemented his command over Venezuela’s oil, following an illegal operation at the start of the year to kidnap President Nicholas Maduro. 

With Iran’s defeat, and Venezuela subjugated, economic rival China would find itself utterly dependent on the US for access to the main lubricant of the global economy. Trump could avoid a direct military confrontation with Beijing, bringing it to heel simply by threatening to turn off the oil spigot. 

But, of course none of this came to pass. 

Washington is now in an unwinnable war with Iran that has clarified to Tehran the extent of its power over the Strait of Hormuz - and of the parallel power of Ansar Allah, its allies in Yemen, over the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Together, they can inflict unmitigated damage to the world economy. 

Soaring petrol prices on US forecourts are likely to be a critical factor in the collapse of the Republican vote in November’s mid-term elections and the likely loss of both Houses to the Democrats, turning Trump into a lame-duck president. 

Meanwhile, the war has educated Washington’s client states in the Gulf that they are supremely vulnerable to any retaliation from Tehran and from Yemen - a fact they are reminded of every time Trump orders another reckless round of strikes on Iran. 

For all its military might, Washington has shown it is unable to defend its Gulf allies.

Facing a reckoning

But Netanyahu is not facing a reckoning just because of his role in engineering a disastrous war on Iran.

Despite the best efforts of western political and media classes over the past three years, the reality of Israel’s destruction of Gaza - and the murder and maiming of many tens of thousands of Palestinian children -  has become ever harder to hide or rationalise. 

Why Netanyahu wants to wreck Trump's Iran deal
Read More »

Even among those parts of the public little interested in world affairs, the truth is gradually sinking in, aided by battles in mainstream cultural spaces that have swung conclusively against Israel. 

NAZA, a new documentary on Gaza made by Israeli film-makers, won a record, 25-minute standing ovation at last month’s Venice Film Festival. In it, anonymised Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers document in detail how they engineered genocide in the tiny enclave. It is scheduled to be available to stream for free in November.

Ireland’s team, forced to play Israel in the Uefa Nations League at the weekend, did not hide their feelings. They wore black armbands in a show of solidarity with Israel’s victims in Gaza and refused to shake hands with their opponents. Irish captain Dara O'Shea pledged to donate his match earnings to humanitarian causes in Gaza. 

Superstar musician Ed Sheeran has found himself unexpectedly painted as the bad guy for failing to stand by his support act, the rapper Macklemore, over the latter’s comments opposing genocide in Gaza. 

Predictably, when faced with pro-Israel stadium owners threatening to pull the plug on the tour, Sheeran caved and dropped Macklemore. But Sheeran is reeling from a widespread backlash that clearly took him by surprise. 

And leading British politicians, such as former prime minister Keir Starmer and foreign secretaries David Cameron and David Lammy, are for the first time facing serious critical scrutiny in the mainstream over their conduct towards Gaza.

Last week, a Channel 4 documentary, Britain’s Gaza Secrets Exposed, revealed that British officials had imposed a deeply flawed methodology, apparently so they could ignore mounting evidence of systematic Israeli war crimes in Gaza. 

As a result, they were able to duck out of their legal obligations to take action against Israel, including by ending arms sales.

Tide of revulsion

Western capitals are finally realising this rising tide of revulsion at the Gaza genocide cannot be staunched. 

In the US, where bonds to Israel are invariably described by politicians as “unbreakable”, 62 percent of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government. 

As elections loom, Naza controversy strikes at the heart of Israel's crisis
Read More »

Meanwhile, a poll last month found 60 percent of American Jews want the Israeli prime minister voted out at the forthcoming election. 

As Israel’s Haaretz newspaper observed: “Trump is well aware of the consistent, dizzying decline in support for Israel among Americans.”

Which is why he and other western politicians are desperate to reframe the conversation. Singling out Netanyahu over Israeli atrocities in Gaza does not get them off the hook because they so obviously partnered with him every step of the way. 

Instead western leaders want to switch focus to the West Bank, where their role is more easily obscured and Netahyahu’s law-breaking is unmistakable. 

Since October 2023, he, along with his self-confessed fascist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have given both violent Jewish settler militias and the Israeli military greater freedom to terrorise Palestinian families off their land in preparation for the West Bank’s annexation. 

In the West’s new, self-serving narrative, Netanyahu isn’t a pariah because he is sought by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in starving the people of Gaza. 

Nor because the International Court of Justice is currently investigating his government over “plausible” allegations that it is committing a genocide in the enclave. 

Nor because his government has overseen the killing of over 21,000 children there - and most likely, far more. 

Nor because he continues to violate a sham “ceasefire”, one in which Israel has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians penned up in the ruins of their enclave since the fighting supposedly ended. A further 4,900 of Gaza’s residents have been maimed over the same period. 

Singling out Netanyahu over Israeli atrocities in Gaza does not get western leaders off the hook because they so obviously partnered with him every step of the way

No, Netanyahu is not a pariah in the eyes of western leaders because of any of these savage crimes - crimes they have been fully complicit in. 

His offence - the one they are now determined to focus attention on - is Netanyahu’s role since October 2023 in intensifying the building and expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank to expel Palestinians from their lands. 

But this narrative works only if western politicians and media studiously ignore the context: that for more than half a century, all Israeli governments sponsored settlement expansion, with the aim of ethnically cleansing the Palestinian population. 

Netanyahu is not an outlier in doing this. He simply exploited the opportunity to accelerate West Bank expulsions on the back of world sympathy after Hamas’s single-day attack in October 2023.

'Ethnic cleansing'

The most likely explanation for why Britain and 11 other western states, including France and Canada, declared their intention last month to impose sanctions on West Bank settlements is that they had received signs from the Trump administration for the first time that there would be no serious repercussions for doing so. 

Britain’s new government under Andy Burnham also dared to describe what Israel has done to West Bank Palestinians as “ethnic cleansing”. Notably, and paradoxically, the UK has avoided using the term to describe Israel’s even more brazen ethnic cleansing in Gaza - a campaign of expulsions that have all too clearly been aided by western bombs and logistics.

War on Iran: How the West is shaping a dystopian era
Read More »

Officials under Mike Huckabee, the fervently partisan US ambassador to Israel, reportedly drafted a stinging rebuke in preparation for the British announcement of sanctions. It accused London of replicating the “playbook of the antisemitic boycott, divestment and sanctions [BDS] movement”. 

That expected line of attack, favoured by Israel lobby groups, was presumably the reason why Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, went to such exaggerated lengths to publicly distance his new policy from BDS. 

But in fact, no attack materialised from the Trump administration. Instead, Marco Rubio, Miliband’s US counterpart, stated innocuously: “I don’t have any comment on it [the sanctions policy] right now.” 

The next day Trump appeared to buy time with a uncharacteristically non-committal response: "I want to find out why all of a sudden has that [the announcement of UK sanctions] happened." 

Trump and Rubio have said nothing more of substance on the matter.

Then there is the recent flood of media reports suggesting that Netanyahu personally failed to listen to multiple warnings from Egypt and the United Arab Emirates that an unprecedented attack was coming from Gaza in the days before Hamas’ break-out on 7 October 2023. 

Netanyahu has called on Abu Dhabi to deny the leaks. But it has so far failed to help out by doing so. 

The two countries, among Washington’s closest client states in the region, have always appeared anxious to avoid openly defying a notoriously vengeful Trump.

Theatre of distraction

In his address to the UN, Burnham noted the dilemma facing western governments: “We live in an age of low trust in politics. If we were to continue to talk about the two-state solution, but fail to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower – and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that.” 

Burnham seems oblivious to the reality: that part of the reason trust is so low is because a succession of British governments have not only colluded in the genocide in Gaza but arrested critics of the genocide as supporters of terrorism. 

Miliband demonstrated precisely the kind of hypocrisy Burnham had warned is alienating the public when he told the Labour Party conference this week - to great applause - that “millions of people in this country”, opponents of the genocide, “were right”. 

They want Netanyahu out of the way not so there is real change but simply so they can revert to what constituted business as usual before the Gaza genocide

The previous day dozens of protesters had been arrested outside the conference venue for silently holding signs stating: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” 

Burnham and Miliband wish to have their cake and eat it. Neither has indicated that there is any intention to scrap the previous government’s decision to use terrorism laws against anyone who holds such a sign - or is “right”, as Miliband now admits. 

What western leaders are engaged in here is the cynical theatre of distraction. 

The declarations of “You were right” and “We feel your pain”, the promises of sanctions and urgent calls for two states, amount to nothing more than virtue-signalling. They are designed to divert public indignation over Israel’s atrocities away from the complicity of western capitals and direct it exclusively at Netanyahu. 

The new spin suggests the gun-wielding, religious zealots in the West Bank settlements who have been growing ever more violent and politically powerful for over half a century - under successive Israeli governments - are solely Netanyahu’s creation. 

The new spin argues that the growing confidence of these pogromists, who have long worked hand in glove with the Israeli military, is entirely unrelated to the West’s unconditional support for Israel over many decades. 

Business as usual

In absolving themselves, however, western leaders are necessarily crafting a new lie to deceive their publics: one that suggests the “settler terrorists” are some kind of personal Netanyahu militia that stands or falls with his premiership.

The implication of this new narrative is that, were Netanyahu to be prised from power, a more empathetic leadership would emerge, one that could be cultivated by western powers to make peace with the Palestinians. 

This is all patent nonsense. 

Like the Israeli public, leaders from across Israel’s narrow Zionist, ethnic supremacist political spectrum shared the genocidal logic that propelled forward the past three-year erasure of Gaza.

None dissented. All engaged in genocidal incitement.

There is no hope of their making peace with the Palestinians under illegal occupation when Israeli leaders cannot even allow their own Palestinian “citizens” - a much-oppressed minority comprising a fifth of Israel’s population - a meaningful voice in next month’s general election.

Those are the competing visions among Israelis for the West Bank: the absolute confinement of Palestinians in a series of cages versus their extermination

The central elections committee, a political body whose members are drawn from Israel’s main parties, voted to ban from standing all four factions representing the Palestinian minority. 

Whoever wins next month’s election, whether Netanyahu again or one of his rivals, will keep the country heading on the same ethnic supremacist track Israel has been on for decades. Trump, Burnham, Macron and other western leaders understand this. 

They want Netanyahu out of the way not so there is real change but simply so they can revert to what constituted business as usual before the Gaza genocide: a slower, more incremental pace to the eradication of the Palestinian people.

They want to be able to rebrand the Gaza genocide as one man’s historic folly, a tragic catastrophe that cannot be reversed but can be mitigated if he is gone. 

They want us looking resolutely forwards, to real-estate deals and a distant two-state solution, not backwards: to their active role in levelling the homes of more than two million people – with mostly US munitions that unleashed eight times the explosive force of the atom bombs that destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The Trump administration has already okayed the shipment of vast numbers of these mega bombs to replenish Israeli stocks, even before the result of the Israeli election is known. 

Notably, the same Trump administration that allowed Netanyahu, a war crimes suspect, to travel to the UN in New York blocked the putative leader of the Palestinians, Mahmoud Abbas, from doing so. 

In announcing his new sanctions policy targeting Israel’s illegal settlements, Miliband was keen to stress that it would in no way affect intelligence sharing with Israel - the kind of intelligence coordination that saw British planes carrying out surveillance operations over Gaza throughout the genocide.

And while Miliband promised a “double lock against arms exports” to Israel as part of the UK’s sanctions package, in practice not a single existing arms export licence has been revoked or suspended since. 

Sinking credibility

The current fight is not against a genocidal Israeli state or for some illusionary Palestinian state - let alone for justice for the endlessly abused Palestinian people.

It is about engineering a reset in which the West gets Israel’s old guard back in charge. 

Labour conference blocks motion to cancel Palantir contract over Israeli army links
Read More »

Western leaders have been embarrassed by the froth-mouthed rantings of Netanyahu’s government. This week Smotrich called for Israel to unleash its genocidal Gaza policies on the West Bank - presumably using the very bombs Trump is about to ship them. 

He told the Israeli media: “We should do there what we did in Gaza.” 

Western leaders fear what that would do to their sinking credibility. And they have allies in Israel, among its opposition, whose vision - at least for the moment - is not Smotrich’s of a Gaza-style eradication of the West Bank.

Rather they envision continuing the current trajectory of gradually turning the West Bank’s small, surviving Palestinian ghettos, trapped in a sea of illegal Jewish settlements, into mini-concentration camps - small replicas of Gaza before it was destroyed. 

Those are the competing visions among Israelis for the West Bank: the absolute confinement of Palestinians in a series of cages versus their extermination. 

That is what is really at stake - nothing more - in the West’s struggle to unseat Netanyahu and uphold its fabled two-state solution.

articles.title: Yemeni army claims 468 operations targeting Houthis killed, wounded hundreds of members
articles.summary:
Yemeni army claims 468 operations targeting Houthis killed, wounded hundreds of members

The Yemeni army claimed it killed and wounded hundreds of Houthi members after its forces carried out 468 operations against the group on three fronts across the country.

Spokesperson Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said the operations targeted Houthi fighters and military equipment on the eastern and Al-Bayda fronts in central Yemen alongside the Al-Mansoura front in Al-Wazi'iyah in the southwest.

"These operations resulted in the killing and injury of hundreds of militia members and the destruction of their military equipment and vehicles," he said.

articles.title: What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
articles.summary:
What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?

A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets. 

The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".

But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.

Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.

The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.

While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.
